title: Relative Clauses
description: Master relative clauses for Grade 8: defining vs non-defining, relative pronouns and adverbs, contact clauses, whose, and prepositions with relatives — bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clauses
topics.concept:
A defining (restrictive) relative clause gives essential information — it tells us which one. It takes no commas, and you may use 'that'.

  • The man who called you is my uncle. (which man? — essential)

A non-defining (non-restrictive) relative clause adds extra, non-essential information. It is set off by commas and cannot use 'that' (use who/which).

  • My father, who is a doctor, works at AIIMS. (we already know which father)

Test: if you can remove the clause and the sentence still identifies the noun, it is non-defining (commas). If removing it leaves the noun unclear, it is defining (no commas).

examples.problem: Defining or non-defining? The book that I bought is torn.
examples.solution: Defining — 'that I bought' tells us which book (essential, no commas).

examples.problem: Punctuate: Mr Rao who teaches us maths is strict. (we know which teacher)
examples.solution: Mr Rao, who teaches us maths, is strict. — extra info needs commas (non-defining).

recap: Non-defining = extra info, commas on both sides, use who/which (not that)
Test: can you remove it and still know which noun?

topics.title: Relative Adverbs, Contact Clauses, Whose & Prepositions
topics.concept:
Relative adverbs replace 'preposition + which':

  • where = in/at which: the house where I live.
  • when = on/at which: the day when we met.
  • why = for which: the reason why he left.

Contact clause (omitting the pronoun): when the relative pronoun is the object of a defining clause, you can drop it.

  • The book (that) I read was great.
  • The man (whom) she married is rich.

whose shows possession (people or things): The student whose essay won was praised.

Preposition + relative: formally, the preposition goes before 'whom/which'; informally, it moves to the end.

  • The friend to whom I wrote replied. (formal) = The friend (who) I wrote to. (informal)

examples.problem: Use a relative adverb: This is the city. I was born in this city.
examples.solution: This is the city where I was born. — 'where' = in which.

examples.problem: Make a contact clause: The pen that you gave me is lost.
examples.solution: The pen you gave me is lost. — drop the object relative 'that'.

recap: Drop an object relative pronoun → contact clause (the book I read)
whose = possession; preposition + whom/which (formal) or end (informal)

questions.q: 'The woman ___ helped me was kind.'
'The phone ___ I bought is new.'
'This is the house ___ we lived.'
Which sentence is non-defining?
options: The dog that bit me ran away.
Mr Roy, who is my neighbour, is friendly.
The pen that I lost was red.

questions.q: 'The student ___ project won is here.'
Which can be omitted (contact clause)?
questions.explanation: An object relative can be dropped: 'the book I read'.

questions.q: 'I'll never forget the day ___ we won.'
Correct the error: 'The man which called is here.'
'My car, ___ is ten years old, still runs.'
Formal: 'The teacher ___ I gave the form is on leave.'
'Tell me the reason ___ you came late.'
Which pronoun fits both people and things in a defining clause?
questions.explanation: 'that' works for people or things (defining only).

questions.q: Combine using a relative clause: 'I have a friend. His brother is an actor.'
options: I have a friend who brother is an actor.
I have a friend whose brother is an actor.
I have a friend which brother is an actor.
I have a friend, his brother is an actor.

questions.q: Choose the correctly punctuated non-defining clause.
options: The Taj Mahal which is in Agra attracts millions.
The Taj Mahal, which is in Agra, attracts millions.
The Taj Mahal, which is in Agra attracts millions.
The Taj Mahal which is in Agra, attracts millions.
questions.explanation: A unique noun takes a non-defining clause with commas on both sides.

questions.q: Reduce the relative clause: 'The boy who is standing there is my brother.'
options: The boy standing there is my brother.
The boy stood there is my brother.
The boy who standing there is my brother.
The boy is standing there my brother.
questions.explanation: 'who is standing' reduces to the participle 'standing'.

questions.q: Spot the error: 'She is the only person who do not agree.'
Choose the formal version: 'This is the house I was born in.'
options: This is the house in which I was born.
This is the house which I was born.
This is the house where in I was born.
This is the house I was born.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly omits the relative pronoun?
options: The man called me is here.
The film we saw was great.
questions.explanation: Only the object relative can be dropped: 'the film (that) we saw'.

questions.q: Rearrange: 'whose / the / honesty / man / admire / all / we'
options: The man whose honesty we all admire.
The man we all admire whose honesty.
Whose honesty the man we all admire.
The man honesty whose we all admire.
questions.explanation: 'The man whose honesty we all admire.' uses possessive 'whose'.

questions.q: Choose the correct relative pronoun: 'Everything ___ glitters is not gold.'

outcomes: Use relative pronouns (who, which, that, whose) correctly
Tell apart defining and non-defining relative clauses
Omit the relative pronoun in contact clauses

intro.en: A relative clause gives more information about a noun, joining two ideas into one neat sentence. Instead of "I met a girl. She won the prize," we say "I met a girl who won the prize." The clause begins with a relative pronoun (who, which, that, whose) or a relative adverb (where, when, why).
intro.hi: संबंधवाचक उपवाक्य (relative clause) किसी संज्ञा के बारे में अधिक जानकारी देता है और दो विचारों को एक साफ़ वाक्य में जोड़ता है। "I met a girl. She won the prize" के बजाय हम कहते हैं "I met a girl who won the prize।" उपवाक्य संबंधवाचक सर्वनाम (who, which, that, whose) या संबंधवाचक क्रिया-विशेषण (where, when, why) से शुरू होता है।

real_life.situation:
You point someone out at a party:

You: That's the man who fixed our car. And this is the house where I grew up. My friend, whose father is a pilot, is coming too.
real_life.why: Each relative clause adds detail to a noun — the man, the house, my friend — without starting a new sentence. 'who' for people, 'where' for places, 'whose' for possession: matching the right relative word is the core skill.

quick_test.q: A non-defining relative clause is set off by:
quick_test.explanation: Non-defining clauses are enclosed in commas.

common_mistakes.wrong: The man which called is my uncle.
common_mistakes.right: The man who called is my uncle.

common_mistakes.wrong: My mother, that is a nurse, works hard.
common_mistakes.right: My mother, who is a nurse, works hard.

common_mistakes.wrong: The house which I live is old.
common_mistakes.right: The house where I live is old.
common_mistakes.note: Use 'where' (= in which) for a place.

common_mistakes.wrong: The girl who her bag was lost cried.
common_mistakes.right: The girl whose bag was lost cried.

reading.passage: The library, which was built a century ago, is the heart of our town. The librarian, whose memory is remarkable, knows every reader who visits. "This is the corner where I first fell in love with books," said an old man whom everyone respects. The day when the new wing opens will be a celebration.

questions.q: Identify a non-defining clause and explain how you know.
questions.answer: "which was built a century ago" — it adds extra info about the library and is set off by commas.

questions.q: Find a relative adverb of place and one of time.
questions.answer: Place: 'where I first fell in love with books'; Time: 'when the new wing opens'.

questions.q: Why is 'whose' used for the librarian?
questions.answer: It shows possession — 'the librarian's memory' becomes 'whose memory'.

speaking: The girl who sits beside me is kind.
This is the book that changed my life.
My friend, whose father is a doctor, is here.
That is the park where we played.
I remember the day when we met.

writing.prompt: Write five sentences about people and places you know, using who, which, whose, where and one non-defining clause (with commas).
writing.example: My teacher, who is very patient, helps everyone. This is the house where I was born.

micro_quiz.q: Make a contact clause: 'The film that we watched was long.'
options: The film we watched was long.
The film what we watched was long.

options: My brother who lives in Pune is a doctor. (one brother)
My brother, who lives in Pune, is a doctor. (one brother)
My brother, who lives in Pune is a doctor.
My brother who lives in Pune, is a doctor.
challenge.explanation: With one brother, the clause is extra info → commas on both sides.

challenge.q: Formal version of 'The person who I spoke to was helpful':
options: The person to whom I spoke was helpful.
The person whom I spoke was helpful.
The person who I spoke was helpful.
The person to who I spoke was helpful.
